note: Every known difference between production Cloud Firestore and another oracle (the emulator, hidane, an SDK's assumption), and what Aruma does. Aruma follows production. Each entry names the test that proves it (test: path:TestName), or the test a later phase writes (planned: {test, phase}), or both; oracle_test.go fails when a named test does not exist, when a planned test's phase is marked closed in phases.json, when a planned test already exists (it then moves to test), and when an evidence file is not pinned by manifest.json. kind is restriction (stricter than Firebase on purpose), provisional (no production evidence yet) or emulator-wrong (Aruma follows production where the emulator errs), the categories of ADR-023 §3 and ADR-028 §7.4. docs/compat/documents-v0.4.md will be generated from this file.

exceptions.summary: The emulator enforces no composite index; production refuses a query whose shape needs one.
exceptions.production: Refuses 45 of the 105 probed shapes with HTTP 400 FAILED_PRECONDITION (gRPC 9) and one of four message templates carrying a console link with the suggested index; the verdict depends on the shape only, the same on a never-written collection (corpus/indexes-105.json).
exceptions.emulator: cloud-firestore-emulator v1.22.0 serves 43 of those 45 and returns the same documents and aggregates as production on the 60 shapes production serves; it refuses orderBy __name__ desc (collection and collection group) with FAILED_PRECONDITION "Firestore does not support descending key scans" where production sends the normal create_composite link for [__name__ DESC] (corpus/indexes-105.emulator.json).
exceptions.aruma: Follows production: composite indexes are enforced by default with production's message bytes and link (plan ADR-025, F3 index/enforce.go), with per-database warn and off modes. Until F3 has a query engine, the test named here pins the recorded difference; F3 adds the replay of corpus/indexes-105.json against Aruma.

exceptions.summary: Query Explain (explain_options on RunQuery and RunAggregationQuery) is rejected in v0.4.0; production supports it on Standard.
exceptions.production: Supports it on REST and gRPC alike (corpus/f0-explain.json). analyze false, or {}: one response element holding only explainMetrics.planSummary, with no document and no readTime. analyze true: the documents as usual, with explainMetrics (planSummary, executionStats with string counts, debugStats as a Struct) on the last document's response. Aggregation: planSummary only, or one element with result, explainMetrics and readTime. A query that needs a composite index gets the normal needs-index error and no metrics.
exceptions.emulator: Not recorded. The Go client's integration suite skips explain and query profiling on the emulator (firestore-clients.md §6).
exceptions.aruma: v0.4.0 answers UNIMPLEMENTED (HTTP 501) with an English message naming Query Explain, after index enforcement, so a query that needs an index gets production's needs-index error first (ADR-025 §5). Ignoring explain_options would crash Node's explain() with "No explain results". Query Explain comes in v0.4.x and must then reproduce the recorded responses. F3 writes the test of the rejection (planned).

exceptions.summary: findNearest is answered with production's exact error when no matching vector index exists, and with UNIMPLEMENTED when one does; production serves it then.
exceptions.production:
With no matching vector index: HTTP 400 FAILED_PRECONDITION (gRPC 9), the same text on REST and gRPC, array-wrapped on REST: "Missing vector index configuration. Please create the required index with the following gcloud command: gcloud firestore indexes composite create --project=

--collection-group= --query-scope=COLLECTION --field-config=vector-config='{"dimension":"","flat": "{}"}',field-path=", with --field-config=order=ASCENDING,field-path= before it for each equality prefilter; the measure and distance options do not appear; a never-written collection gets the same text (corpus/f0-find-nearest.json). With a matching vector index production runs the search (docs; not recorded, since the oracle may not create indexes).
exceptions.aruma: No matching vector index: production's status and message byte for byte. Matching vector index (stored and returned by the Admin API since v0.4.0): UNIMPLEMENTED (HTTP 501) naming findNearest. An exact-scan implementation comes in v0.4.x (ADR-025 §5, ADR-028 §3). F3 writes the test (planned).

exceptions.summary: A query inside a pessimistic read-write transaction locks the whole collection under its parent (a collection-group query: the collection id across the database), coarser than production's range locks.
exceptions.production: Locks the index range a query scans (corpus/f2-locks.json, two runs, every outcome stable): with T1 holding `n > 3` on c/A/sub, a plain commit that updates a matched document, inserts a document with n in the range (a phantom), or moves a document into it waits until T1 ends (about 20 s, then ABORTED "Too much contention on these documents. Please try again.", corpus/f0-contention.json s6); an insert below the range, an insert without the field, an update of an unmatched document, a write to c/B/sub (same collection id, other parent) and a write to another collection do not wait. A whole-collection query blocks inserts into that collection but not into c/B/sub; `orderBy n limit 2` blocks inserts both before the first and after the last returned document; a collection-group query blocks inserts under any parent with that collection id but not into another collection id.
exceptions.emulator: Locks the collection id for every query in a read-write transaction, so writes to every collection with that id wait (measured by hidane; firestore-prior-art-and-verification.md §A2).
exceptions.aruma: A collection query or ListDocuments with a collection id takes a shared lock on (parent path, collection id); a collection-group query takes it on the collection id across the database; a kindless query or ListDocuments with an empty collection id takes it on the database. Every write takes intention locks on all three (ADR-024 §6.1, ADR-025 §7.3). Only service-account and admin pessimistic transactions that run queries are affected: end-user transactions are optimistic and hold no locks while open. Coarser than production where a write outside the scanned range of the same collection (an insert below the range or without the field, an update of an unmatched document) waits on Aruma and not on production; a phantom insert, a matched update and the sibling-parent and other-collection writes behave as production. Until F3 runs queries, the test shows it with a listing, which takes the lock a whole-collection query takes: a phantom insert and an update of a listed document wait, an insert below the range, one without the field and an update of an unmatched document wait on Aruma alone, and the sibling-parent and other-collection writes do not wait.

exceptions.summary: Transactions open when Aruma restarts (or loses its Document Database instance lock) are lost; their authentic ids get ABORTED, so clients retry.
exceptions.production: Production does not restart under a client. An id that never existed, a forged id (last byte flipped) and an empty id get INVALID_ARGUMENT "Invalid transaction." on commit, GET, runQuery and rollback (corpus/f0-errors.json, corpus/f2-transactions.json); a committed or rolled-back id gets HTTP 409 ABORTED "The referenced transaction has expired or is no longer valid." (corpus/f0-errors.json, corpus/f0-contention.json s5, corpus/f2-transactions.json). Lifetime (corpus/f2-transactions.json `lifetime`): a read-write transaction is usable at 241 s and gets that ABORTED text at 271 s whether it was idle or read every 30 s (the lifetime runs from begin, not from the last use); at 300 s an id idle since its begin, read-write or read-only, gets INVALID_ARGUMENT "Invalid transaction.", as an id that never existed. Idle for 70 s, a transaction still holds its read lock: a plain write waits about 20 s and gets ABORTED "Too much contention on these documents. Please try again.", and the transaction then commits.
exceptions.emulator: Keeps transactions in memory; a restart loses them with all data.
exceptions.aruma: Transaction ids carry an HMAC under a key derived from the master key, over a format version, a per-process boot nonce, a serial, the issue time, and the project, database and principal. A forged, garbage or foreign id gets INVALID_ARGUMENT "Invalid transaction." as production. An authentic id unknown to this process (issued before a restart or before the instance lock was lost) or expired gets ABORTED "The referenced transaction has expired or is no longer valid.", on which Go and Node retry with a fresh age (ADR-025 §7.5, ADR-024 §6.2). Expiry follows the recorded lifetime: ABORTED with that text from 270 s after begin; from 300 s after begin (the issue time in the id) every id is forgotten and gets INVALID_ARGUMENT "Invalid transaction.", as production's. The difference left is the restart itself: within 300 s of its begin, a transaction lost by a restart answers ABORTED where production's would still be open.

exceptions.summary: A REQUEST_TIME transform's value is the commit's commit_time at whole milliseconds, not the time the request arrived.
exceptions.production: Recorded (corpus/f2-transforms.json st.*, corpus/f2-transactions.json time.commit): the value has millisecond precision (3 fraction digits; gRPC nanos a multiple of 10^6) and is not the commitTime nor the commitTime truncated: it is 5 to 27 ms before the commitTime (once, with a delete of the same document in the commit, 140 ms after). The stored value equals the transform result; every REQUEST_TIME of one commit (several fields, several documents, two writes to one document) is the same value; two concurrent commits got different values.
exceptions.aruma: RequestTime(commit_time): the commit's own commit_time, which Postgres's clock_timestamp() gives under the sequencer row (ADR-024 §2.1), rounded down to the millisecond (core/transforms.go). It keeps every recorded invariant: millisecond precision, one value for the whole commit, the stored value equal to the result. It is stricter on purpose: the value is never after the commitTime (production's once was) and follows the commits' order, from the one clock that orders them. It costs a commit with REQUEST_TIME one extra round trip: the stamp goes alone, the documents are built with the commit_time it returns, then the rest of the commit is sent, while the commit holds the sequencer row (core/sequencer.go stamp); a commit without REQUEST_TIME sends its stamp, documents and COMMIT in one. It differs from production's by the few milliseconds between the request's arrival and its commit; two commits within one millisecond may share a value.

exceptions.summary: A Commit or BatchWrite holds at most 10,000 writes and 50,000 field transforms, and a commit rebuilds at most 2^22 values of documents it already wrote; over them it is refused with INVALID_ARGUMENT and Aruma's own text.
exceptions.production: Accepted one commit and one batchWrite of 501 updates (corpus/f2-commit.json and corpus/f2-batch-write.json limit.501_writes). Its bounds above that, on writes, field transforms and the work of many writes of one large document, are not recorded; its documented 10 MiB request limit is not recorded either.
exceptions.aruma: Bounds the work a request makes before its rules and size checks by count as well as by bytes (documents.limits.message_bytes): 10,000 writes per request and 50,000 field transforms across its writes (api/writes.go MaxRequestWrites, MaxRequestTransforms: "A request may hold at most 10000 writes.", "A request may hold at most 50000 field transforms."), and 2^22 values (one more per 16 bytes) of the top-level fields a commit's writes rebuild in documents an earlier write of the commit already wrote (core/writes.go MaxCommitWork: "The commit's writes rebuild more than 4194304 values of documents they already wrote. Please split it into smaller commits."), about a second of one core. Every recorded case is far within them: none writes a document more than twice. Record production's answers to 10,000 and 100,000 writes and to 20,000 transforms to replace the texts.

exceptions.summary: A Listen target resumed from a resume token or read_time older than the one-hour version window: the count path for targets without limit or offset, RESET plus the full current set for targets with either.
exceptions.production: Not recorded. The client libraries handle an ExistenceFilter count mismatch by re-querying, and the backend sending a filter on resume is an inference from an integration test (firestore-clients.md §1.8 item 7). To be recorded in F4 with a token kept for more than an hour (ADR-028 §7.6).
exceptions.emulator: Restarts every resumed target from scratch: RESET and the full result (firestore-prior-art-and-verification.md §A2).
exceptions.aruma: Without limit or offset: the documents now matching with update_time after T, then ExistenceFilter{count} of the exact current matches, then CURRENT; correct because the current result is a subset of what the client held plus what was sent. With limit or offset, where that fails at the window edge: RESET, the full current result, then CURRENT (ADR-026 §1.5; MUST 7 allows both). Never an error. F4's Listen reference model tests it (planned), with a limit target resuming past the window after a member was deleted.

exceptions.summary: A query that needs a composite index which exists but is still CREATING gets the needs-index error until production's answer is recorded.
exceptions.production: Not recorded: the oracle may not create indexes on the production project. Production answers such a query with its own index-building response, to be recorded with R18 to R22 in a project where indexes may be created (ADR-025 §4.2, ADR-028 §7.6).
exceptions.emulator: Enforces no index (see emulator-index-enforcement), so it serves the query.
exceptions.aruma: An index is created CREATING; from then every commit also writes its entries, the existing documents are backfilled in key-range batches, and it becomes READY only after the backfill (ADR-024 §2.5). The planner never uses a CREATING index; until production's response is recorded the query gets the needs-index error (template 1). F3's index tests cover it (planned).

exceptions.summary: A Listen target or a later Write-stream message naming another database than the stream's is refused with Aruma's modelled answer until production's is recorded; for unary RPCs Aruma matches production's recorded text.
exceptions.production:
Recorded for unary RPCs (corpus/f1-resource-names.json): a Commit write or a BatchGet document of another project, or of another database of the same project, is refused with HTTP 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT (gRPC 3) "The request was for database 'projects/

/databases/' but was attempting to access database 'projects//databases/'", on REST and gRPC alike; a commit holding one good write and one foreign write is refused whole, naming the foreign database; a google-cloud-resource-prefix naming another project is ignored when the body names the database (gRPC Commit and GetDocument succeed). Not recorded: a Listen add_target, or a Write-stream message after the first, naming another database (F4, ADR-028 §7.6).
exceptions.aruma: Unary RPCs match production: wire.Bind takes the request's database from its first name (the REST path's, or the database field), refuses one the caller is not entitled to with PERMISSION_DENIED (ADR-029 §3 rule 6), and answers every later name of another database with production's INVALID_ARGUMENT text; google-cloud-resource-prefix is never bound against the body, as production ignores it (TestBindResourceNamesF1 replays every recorded case). Provisional part: a Listen target naming another database is REMOVE with that INVALID_ARGUMENT as its cause, the stream staying open (ADR-026 §1.3, ADR-027 §2.2), and a later Write-stream message naming another database is refused with the same INVALID_ARGUMENT (TestBindIsolation); F4 records production's answers and replays them (planned).

exceptions.summary: A query with more than ten inequality fields is refused with production's status and text, but the fields its message lists are in the request's order, where production lists them in an order of its own.
exceptions.production: Refuses eleven inequality fields f0 … f10 with HTTP 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT (gRPC 3) "The query contains 11 distinct inequality fields: [f8, f9, f6, f7, f4, f5, f2, f3, f0, f1, f10]. A query may not have more than 10 distinct inequality fields.", on REST and gRPC alike (corpus/f3-query-limits.json ineq.11_fields, grpc.ineq_11_fields). The order is neither the request's, nor sorted, nor a Java HashSet's of the field names; one recorded set does not show its rule.
exceptions.aruma: The same status and text, the fields listed in the order the request first names them (query/validate.go errInequalityFields, F3): "[f0, f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, f6, f7, f8, f9, f10]" for the recorded query. The two recorded cases are listed as differing in the F3 replays, which fail once they match. Record more sets of field names to find production's order.
